headline: All of Canada’s Big Six Banks Now See December Rate Hike
author: Mario Baker Ramirez and Erik Hertzberg

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Canada's six largest lenders all expect the central bank to hike its key interest rate in December, even with two major economic releases still to come next week.

Economists brought forward their rate calls after Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem reinforced concerns about persistent inflation during public remarks Tuesday. He emphasized the risk that companies will pass higher energy costs on to consumers.

Toronto-Dominion Bank, the final major Canadian bank to change its forecast to call for a hike next month, said Macklem's comments on better-than-expected economic resilience suggest policymakers are "more concerned about what is to come."
"The hike looks to be a move focused on managing inflation risks," TD Senior Economist Andrew Hencic said in an email Wednesday.

Earlier this week, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and Bank of Montreal said they now expect a hike in December rather than January. Bank of Nova Scotia, Royal Bank of Canada and National Bank of Canada were already forecasting a December hike.
The central bank raised its policy rate to 2.5% in October, the first increase in three years, as high energy costs stemming from the ongoing conflict in the Middle East added to inflation pressures.
Markets also appear convinced another hike will be announced in December, with traders in overnight swaps putting the odds at about 80% as of Wednesday afternoon.

That conviction comes before the national statistics agency publishes quarterly gross domestic product data and the November jobs report, two key readings that will give policymakers a final look at the strength of the economy before their decision.
Macklem warned Tuesday that higher energy costs are likely to pass through to consumer prices, even as oil prices have recently eased.

BMO strategist Benjamin Reitzes said there's still uncertainty about what happens beyond December's meeting, "but the speech doesn't talk about neutral or provide any sign that they're looking to pause after another hike."

Macklem's comments also prompted economists to reassess how the central bank may respond to future supply shocks. The bank's updated approach suggests policymakers may react more quickly and put greater emphasis on headline inflation in its communications, said Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics.
The Bank of Canada's next rate decision is on Dec. 9.
